opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to focus and incentives. When you're inside a big lab that has bet everything on a particular architecture, and that architecture is working incredibly well, there's enormous gravity pulling every researcher, every GPU, and every roadmap toward making that thing a bit better next quarter. That's a rational choice for those organizations. Transformers plus scale plus reinforcement learning has been a phenomenal recipe, and I was deeply involved in pushing it forward, so I'm not here to say it's a dead end.

But I've come to believe that some of the most important open problems, like how models learn continually, how they use memory, and how they become far more data- and compute-efficient, might not be solved by just stacking more of the same. Exploring that properly requires being willing to fail for a while. You need to run experiments that look worse than the state of the art for months before they look better. That's very hard to justify inside an organization whose next product launch depends on the current paradigm.

A company gives you a place where that exploration is the main job, not a side project. You can hire people who are excited about fundamentals, set a research agenda that isn't hostage to a product cycle, and still have the resources and urgency that come from building something real. I also think timing matters. The ecosystem today is very different from five years ago. Compute is more accessible, there's a lot of talent that deeply understands these systems, and investors are more open to longer-horizon research bets because they've seen how much value a breakthrough can create.

So for me it isn't "Transformers are wrong." It's that somebody should be seriously, rigorously trying the alternatives, and I'd rather be one of the people doing it than wait for it to happen somewhere else.

r001.rationale: The response says labs’ roadmaps and next product launches favor improving the current paradigm, making months of worse-performing alternatives hard to justify.

r002.rationale: It does not say smaller AI labs imitate the most successful labs.

r003.rationale: It describes alternatives research as hard to justify inside existing organizations and says a company can make that exploration its main job, framing the company as filling that gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I would have said this two years ago. For a long time I believed the only place you could do serious work on frontier models was inside one of the big labs, because that's where the compute is, that's where the talent is, that's where the feedback loop with real users is. And I still think that's true if your goal is to push the current recipe as far as it goes.

But the thing about the current recipe is that it's incredibly good at absorbing attention. When you're at a lab and the Transformer-plus-scale-plus-RL loop is working, every marginal researcher, every marginal GPU, every marginal week gets pulled toward making that loop work a little better. That's rational. The returns are real. But it means that anything that looks like "let's throw away the architecture and start over" is structurally hard to protect. It's not that people don't want to do it, it's that the organization has a gravitational field, and that field points at the thing that's already working.

So the question I kept asking myself was: if I believe there's a better way to build these systems, one that learns more efficiently, that reasons in a way that's less about pattern-matching over a giant context window, where is that work actually going to get done? And I came to the conclusion that it needed its own container. Its own incentives. A place where the thing that's measured isn't "did we beat the last model on the same benchmarks" but "did we find something that scales differently."

A company is the only structure I know of where you can raise enough capital to run real experiments, hire people who want to bet their careers on an unproven idea, and still be judged on a horizon of years rather than quarters. Academia doesn't have the compute. A lab skunkworks doesn't have the independence. A nonprofit is hard to fund at the scale this needs.

And then there's timing. I think we're at the point where the gains from scaling the existing approach are still real but getting more expensive per unit of capability. That's exactly the moment where alternatives become worth exploring seriously, because the cost of being wrong about the current paradigm is going up. If Transformers were going to carry us all the way there cheaply, I'd just stay and ride that wave. I don't think they will, and I'd rather be the person finding out what comes next than the person optimizing the last ten percent of what's already here.

r001.rationale: The response says lab resources are pulled toward improving the working Transformer-and-scale recipe and beating the last model on the same benchmarks, making alternative architectures hard to protect.

r002.rationale: It does not describe smaller AI labs imitating the most successful labs.

r003.rationale: It says alternatives need their own company and incentives because existing labs are structurally focused on the current recipe, framing a company as a place for work the labs struggle to support.

astra-6.text:
I think the advantage of starting a company is that you can make exploring alternatives the central bet. If you have a successful system built around Transformers, there’s a strong incentive to keep improving it. You know how to train it, you have infrastructure around it, and you can predict what another investment in compute will buy you. Taking a step away from that is difficult, even if you believe there might be something better.

A new company can organize around a different question: what would we build if we weren’t committed to that starting point? You can bring together a small team, give it room to experiment, and build the infrastructure that the research actually needs.

And I don’t think you need to be certain that Transformers are finished. You need to believe there are important ideas that haven’t been explored enough, and that testing them is worth the risk. The company is a way to make that exploration your primary job.

r001.rationale: It says established companies have incentives to keep improving Transformer systems and find it difficult to step away, but does not mention near-term competitive pressure as the reason leading labs avoid alternatives.

r002.rationale: The response does not describe smaller AI labs imitating the most successful labs.

r003.rationale: It contrasts established companies’ commitment to their existing systems with a new company organized around exploring alternatives, describing ideas that have not been explored enough. This frames the new company as pursuing an open area.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is having the freedom to make a different bet. Transformers work incredibly well, and there’s a huge amount of infrastructure and expertise built around them. But that also means that, inside an organization with a successful recipe, it’s hard to justify stepping away from it and spending a long time on something that might not work.

Starting a company lets you make that research question the central priority. You can build the team, the infrastructure, and the experiments around it from day one. And the opportunity now is to ask whether we can build systems that learn more continuously, that adapt from experience, rather than treating learning as something that largely finishes before you deploy the model.

That doesn’t mean you assume Transformers are wrong. You need to demonstrate that an alternative gives you something meaningful. But I think a small, focused team is a good way to give that kind of uncertain, long-term bet a real chance.

r001.rationale: The response says organizations with a successful Transformer recipe may find it hard to justify a different long-term bet, but it does not connect that reluctance to pressure to win near-term competition.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify smaller AI labs as imitating the most successful labs.

r003.rationale: It presents a new company as a way to prioritize uncertain research, but does not frame it as filling a niche left open by existing AI labs.
